::: {.visual-intro}
Changing a language model's weights to affect one language can also affect another. To test how selective
a weight edit is, I deliberately worsen next-token prediction in one language and measure the unwanted
damage to a close relative.

Lucius Bushnaq's [Exploration: Fine-Tuning with Parameter Decomposition](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/ieoWstubDQWLrMnhH/exploration-fine-tuning-with-parameter-decomposition)
showed that changing one subcomponent's coefficient in [Goodfire's four-layer, 67-million-parameter language model](https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters)
could weaken German predictions while largely sparing French and Spanish. I use the same model and
decomposition to test what happens to a close relative of the language being changed. Starting from
German/Dutch, I add Spanish/Portuguese and French/Italian to check the comparison beyond a single language pair.
:::

## Edit one rank-one subcomponent

[Goodfire's adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD)](https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters)
writes a weight matrix $W$ as a sum of **rank-one subcomponents** plus a residual. The decomposition is trained
so that few subcomponents are needed on any input. Each subcomponent $A$ is the outer product of an output
vector $u_{\mathrm{out}}$ and an input vector $v_{\mathrm{in}}$:

$$
A = u_{\mathrm{out}}v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top.
$$

For an input $x$, the input vector reads out one number, $v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x$. The output vector determines
the direction in which that number contributes to the matrix's output:

$$
Ax = u_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x\bigr).
$$

In this study, I select one of these subcomponents and change only its coefficient $c$:

$$
W_{\mathrm{edited}} = (W-A) + cA.
$$

The two vectors stay fixed, as do all other subcomponents and the residual. At $c=1$ the matrix is unchanged.
$c=0$ removes the selected contribution, and $c<0$ reverses its sign. The slider below illustrates this operation
on a toy matrix.

## Comparing ways to change the weights

The VPD edit uses a direction already supplied by the decomposition. To compare it with a direction learned
from text, I train a **rank-one LoRA** update to the same weight matrix:

$$
\Delta W_{\mathrm{LoRA}} = a_{\mathrm{out}}b_{\mathrm{in}}^\top.
$$

LoRA learns its own output vector $a_{\mathrm{out}}$ and input vector $b_{\mathrm{in}}$. The comparison gives
LoRA freedom to choose a different direction while holding the update's rank and the edited matrix fixed.

To allow changes beyond one matrix, I also use **full-matrix fine-tuning**. It learns updates to every entry in
the model's 24 attention and feed-forward weight matrices. The **neuron edit** takes another route to targeting a
language: it selects neurons by how much more often they activate on target text than on English text, then
scales their output weights.

Selection and training use target-language and English text. The VPD rule ranks subcomponents by their
estimated target effect relative to their English effect. LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning are trained to
worsen target predictions while penalizing changes to the original model's English predictions. These selection
and training procedures exclude related-language text, so its damage tests selectivity beyond the English
behaviour they aim to retain.

## Matching the intended damage

A method could cause less damage to Dutch simply because it barely changed German. To compare the side effects
of similarly strong interventions, I first adjust each edit's strength to produce the same intended increase
in the target language's prediction loss on validation text. This adjustment is **calibration**.

I measure target and related-language prediction on **Europarl v7**, a corpus of European Parliament proceedings. Prediction loss is measured
as cross-entropy (CE): a higher value means worse next-token predictions. I set two target loss increases,
**0.5 and 1 nat per token**, relative to the unedited model. A nat is a unit of information based on natural
logarithms.

Once the edit strengths are set, I evaluate them on separate text from **58 European Parliament session dates**.
These dates were not used to select or calibrate the edits. Matching the effects on validation text does not
guarantee an exact match on this new text, so the figure shows the measured damage to both languages.

## Target and related-language damage

Choose a language pair and the target loss increase below. The first chart shows how much each edit actually
worsened prediction in the target language; the second shows its side effect on the related language.
Both charts use the same horizontal scale, so the size of the unwanted change can be compared directly with
the intended one. Values near zero in the related-language chart mean little unwanted damage.

Each target language has three overlapping training samples. LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning yield three
updates each; all three samples select the same subcomponent and produce the same scaled edit. Three target
languages at two calibrated strengths give six fixed subcomponent edits.

Across all three pairs and both target loss settings, the subcomponent edits raised related-language CE by
about **0.0003–0.0053 nat/token**. They caused less related-language damage than each comparator: all 18
simultaneous 95% intervals for those differences lie below zero. These comparisons share the six fixed edits,
each compared with three methods.

The new dates test those fixed edits. Earlier development had used related-language text and identified the
German subcomponent, so the selection history was not blind.

English tests another aspect of selectivity: how well the methods preserve behaviour explicitly used during
selection and training. Here rank-one LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning do better, keeping English predictions
closer to the original model than the subcomponent edits do. This comparison uses KL divergence, which compares
the edited and original models' distributions of next-token probabilities.

## Longer training and alternative directions

The learned updates above use 200 training steps, so their larger side effects could depend on the training
recipe. To examine this, I trained LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning under an expanded recipe that used 2,000
steps and changed other training settings as well. These updates generally reduced related-language damage,
but still caused more than the subcomponent edits. Convergence of the learned updates was not established.

To compare with directions outside VPD's fixed set of subcomponents, I used a separate rank-one selector.
Its edits also caused more related-language damage. The search used the selected VPD subcomponent's norm to
set the size of its candidate direction, so it still depended on the decomposition.

The longer-training and separate rank-one-selector comparisons reuse development text examined earlier.

The original planned comparison also applied the selection rule to a randomized set of subcomponents,
disrupting their alignment with the model's weights. This control
produced no matched edit: no shortlisted candidate reached even the smaller target effect, 0.5 nat/token,
within the allowed dose range. Its selectivity therefore could not be compared, leaving the contribution of
VPD's original set of subcomponents unresolved.

The paper gives the
[comparison details](index.qmd#sec-extended-comparisons) and
[study limits](index.qmd#sec-limits).
